stations.title: THE FIRST SEASON
stations.claim: Core Claim 1 — the sites are underground because of cataclysm, not deliberate burial
stations.anchor: Klaus Schmidt of the German Archaeological Institute recognised the T-pillars in 1994 and opened excavation in 1995. The enclosures lay under as much as fifteen metres of fill. Since 2018 the DAI's own team (Lee Clare and colleagues) has questioned the 'deliberate backfill' reading and proposed slope-slide and natural infill.
stations.check: Schmidt, Sie bauten die ersten Tempel (2006); Clare, L., 'Göbekli Tepe, Turkey: a brief summary of research at a new World Heritage Site (2015–2019)', e-Forschungsberichte DAI 2020.
stations.setting: the tell at Göbekli Tepe in its first season, string grids pegged across a low mound of packed fill, the head of a T-shaped limestone pillar just breaking the surface, wheelbarrows and sieves, a German archaeologist in a brimmed hat kneeling at the stone with a brush.
stations.hook: a brush already sweeping dust off a T-shaped stone head
stations.natori: Nineteen ninety-five. He brushed the dirt off a T-shaped head & the whole timeline moved.
stations.rogue: Fifteen metres of fill. Nobody carries that much dirt uphill on purpose.
stations.score: a single low cello note held under the hook, rising a fifth at the turn and settling back onto the note it opened on; a dry frame drum ticks once per second beneath it.

sfx.text: wind humming through the grid strings

stations.title: THE TRENCH
stations.claim: Core Claim 2 — Kenyon's Pre-Pottery Neolithic scheme frames all Near-Eastern dating
stations.anchor: Kathleen Kenyon dug Tell es-Sultan from 1952 to 1958 and defined the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B phases that Near-Eastern chronology still uses, working in five-metre squares with standing baulks (the Wheeler–Kenyon method).
stations.check: Kenyon, Digging Up Jericho (1957); Kenyon, Excavations at Jericho, vols I–V (1960–1983).
stations.setting: Kenyon's deep trench at Tell es-Sultan cut in five-metre squares with earth baulks standing between them, tags and string on every face, the top of the round stone tower emerging, a woman in a shirt and skirt with a clipboard directing workmen in kufiyas.
stations.hook: a bucket of spoil already rising on a rope out of the square
stations.natori: Nineteen fifty-two, Jericho. One woman, one trench, & every Near-Eastern date since is set by her ladder.
stations.rogue: Pre-Pottery A, Pre-Pottery B. The rungs were hers.
stations.score: a slow metronomic woodblock at walking pace under a sustained viola line; the viola climbs one step at each of her words and comes back down under his.

stations.title: THE FIRST ACCOUNTS
stations.claim: Core Claim 3 — cylinder seals and proto-writing are dated 3500–3100 BC everywhere but Göbekli Tepe
stations.anchor: The Uruk IV tablets (about 3350–3200 BC) are the earliest writing known. Cylinder seals appear at Uruk and Susa about 3500 BC; seals inscribed with personal names come only in the Early Dynastic period, about 2600 BC.
stations.check: Nissen, Damerow & Englund, Archaic Bookkeeping (1993); the Uruk tablets on the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (cdli.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de).
stations.setting: a ramp climbing the Eanna temple platform at Uruk, scribes on the steps pressing reed styluses into wet clay tablets, drilled stone cylinders being rolled across clay sealings, kilns smoking below the platform.
stations.hook: a stone cylinder already rolling across wet clay
stations.natori: Uruk, thirty-three hundred. Wet clay, a reed, & the first account anyone ever kept.
stations.rogue: The rule says seals this old are impossible. The rule was written here.
stations.score: a reed flute phrase over a low tanpura-like drone; the phrase is played forward under her line and in retrograde under his, ending on its first note.

stations.title: THE TABLETS
stations.claim: Core Claim 4 — rongorongo is used to date Easter Island young while writing at Göbekli Tepe changes nothing
stations.anchor: Brother Eugène Eyraud's letter of December 1864 is the first report of the rongorongo tablets; about twenty-six survive. In 2024 a radiocarbon study dated the wood of one tablet to the fifteenth century, before any European landing.
stations.check: Eyraud in Annales de la Propagation de la Foi 38 (1866); Ferrara, S. et al., 'The invention of writing on Rapa Nui', Scientific Reports 14 (2024).
stations.setting: a missionary's thatched hut on a windswept slope, a lay brother in a black cassock turning an incised wooden tablet over in his hands by lamplight, islanders watching from the doorway, the backs of stone giants on the ridge behind.
stations.hook: a wooden tablet already turning in lamplight, rows of signs catching the flame
stations.natori: Eighteen sixty-four. A lay brother writes home about wooden boards covered in signs.
stations.rogue: One board dates before any European landed. The writing is theirs. They still say young.
stations.score: wind-harp tones with a single bowed bass note; the bass drops a tritone under 'young' and resolves back up to the opening pitch.

stations.title: THE SEATED MAN
stations.claim: Core Claim 5 — Karahan Tepe carries an apkallu supporting a winged disc, a 2600 BC+ motif
stations.anchor: Systematic excavation began in 2019 under Necmi Karul. In September 2023 the team announced a 2.3-metre seated male statue and a life-size vulture statue. The site lies about forty kilometres east of Göbekli Tepe. The apkallu-with-winged-disc reading is Breshears'; the site, the dig and the statues are the checkable part.
stations.check: Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism, statement of 30 September 2023; Karul, N., 'Buried buildings at Pre-Pottery Neolithic Karahantepe', Türk Arkeoloji ve Etnografya Dergisi 82 (2021).
stations.setting: the sunken rock-cut chamber at Karahan Tepe with its forest of tall pillars carved straight out of the bedrock, a huge seated stone man with his ribs showing being lifted from the fill, a stone vulture beside him, the path spiralling down into the pit.
stations.hook: a stone man already rising out of the fill on straps
stations.natori: Twenty twenty-three. A man carved from the living rock sits up in his own pit.
stations.rogue: Forty kilometres from the first hill. Same hands. Same posture. Same silence.
stations.score: a low brass pedal with a slow struck bell every three seconds; the bell is left to ring out into the settle.

sfx.text: gravel sliding down the pit wall

stations.title: THE BENNU

stations.title: THE KINGFISHER
stations.claim: Core Claim 15 — the bird plucking a fish carries one meaning from Cyprus to Nazca to New Mexico
stations.anchor: Classic Mimbres bowls (about 1000–1130 AD) painted with birds catching fish are held in museum collections, many with a 'kill hole' punched through the centre for burial. Cypro-Archaic free-field jugs (about 750–600 BC) carry the same bird-with-fish. The shared meaning is the claim; the motif's presence in both places is checkable.
stations.check: Brody, Mimbres Painted Pottery (rev. 2004); Karageorghis, Ancient Art from Cyprus: The Cesnola Collection (Metropolitan Museum, 2000).
stations.setting: a descent along the river into a Mimbres pithouse village, a potter painting a black-on-white bowl with a long-legged bird lifting a fish, finished bowls with holes knocked through their centres stacked beside an open grave, cottonwoods along the water.
stations.hook: a brush already drawing the curve of a bird's neck on white clay
stations.natori: New Mexico, ten fifty. A bowl with a bird lifting a fish, & a hole knocked through the middle.
stations.rogue: Cyprus. Nazca. Babylon. One bird, one fish, one message.
stations.score: a cedar flute over water-drum, the flute's four-note call answered by itself upside down and ending on the call's first note.
